description: C++ solution sorting by start time, merging in-place with O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space.

transcript.text: Hello! If intervals are not sorted initially, adjacent intervals might not be contiguous in the array. So the first step is sorting by start time. That takes O(n log n).
Good observation. How will you merge them after sorting?

We maintain our merged list. For each interval, if merged is empty or current.start > merged.back().end, there is no overlap, so we push it. Otherwise, there is an overlap, so merged.back().end = max(merged.back().end, current.end).
What edge cases did you consider?

1. Empty or single interval array. 2. Completely non-overlapping intervals. 3. One interval fully inside another like [1, 5] and [2, 3]. 4. Touching boundaries like [1, 4] and [4, 6] which should merge into [1, 6].
